prior_art.basis: Independent review by claude-independent-prior-art-reviewer-20261106: No open or discoverable network detects any new outbreak within 24 hours, so the Main KPI of 195 countries covered by 24-hour pathogen early warning is unmet; the accepted global target is detection within 7 days, and it is often missed. A retrospective 7-1-7 review in five countries found only 22 of 41 public health events (54%) detected within 7 days, with a median of 6 days and a range of 0 to 157 days (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:37060911&resultType=core&format=json); in Uganda, longer time to detection across 84 outbreaks was linked to more cases and deaths (https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjgh-2025-020034). WHO's EIOS system, used by 120 countries and 30 organisations by end-2025, offers near-real-time open-source intelligence but publishes no detection-time metrics (https://www.who.int/initiatives/eios); an evaluation framework was published only in 2026 (https://doi.org/10.2807/1560-7917.es.2026.31.5.2500363). Aircraft wastewater networks are proposed for global monitoring (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-025-03501-4). GitHub has one small event-based-surveillance project. Honest limit: event-based surveillance, ProMED-style reporting and wastewater sequencing are known, so tasks that re-implement them are not new work; 24-hour detection of any new pathogen also needs diagnostics and sampling, not only intelligence, so tasks must target a checkable piece such as measured time-to-detection gains on historical outbreaks.
